title: Recognise pests, diseases and weeds on crops

lessons.title: Insects and other animals
lessons.html:
Is it an insect?

Many small animals live on crops. Some are insects, some are not. You must know the difference to report correctly.

An insect has

  • Three body parts: head, thorax (middle) and abdomen (back part).
  • Six legs, all on the thorax.
  • Two antennae (feelers) on the head.
  • Usually wings (one or two pairs) on the thorax as adults.

Other small animals that are not insects

AnimalHow to tell
SpidersEight legs, two body parts, no antennae
Mites (red spider mite)Tiny, eight legs; leave fine webs and speckled leaves
Snails and slugsNo legs, soft body, slime trail
MillipedesMany legs, long body
Nematodes (eelworms)Tiny worms in the soil; cause root knots

Parts of an insect that damage crops

  • Chewing mouthparts on the head (caterpillars, beetles, grasshoppers, locusts): they bite and eat leaves, stems, fruit and roots.
  • Sucking mouthparts like a needle (aphids, whitefly, stink bugs, scale, mealybugs): they suck plant juice.
  • Egg-laying parts at the end of the abdomen (for example fruit flies): they push eggs into fruit.

Using a hand lens

Many pests are very small. A hand lens (magnifying glass) helps you count legs and see mites, thrips and aphid nymphs. Carry one when you scout, and look on the underside of leaves, where many pests hide from the sun.

Not all insects are pests, not all pests are insects

  • Beneficial insects help the farmer: ladybirds and lacewings eat aphids, parasitic wasps kill caterpillars, bees pollinate. Do not kill them.
  • Pests that are not insects: mites, snails, nematodes, birds, rats, porcupines, baboons and weeds.

lessons.title: Insect life cycles and damage
lessons.html:
How insects grow

Insects change shape as they grow. There are two main life cycles.

Complete change (four stages)

Egg, larva, pupa, adult. The larva looks very different from the adult.

  • Moths and butterflies: the larva is a caterpillar, for example the fall armyworm and the maize stalk borer.
  • Beetles: the larva is a grub, for example white grubs in the soil.
  • Flies: the larva is a maggot, for example fruit fly maggots in fruit.

Often the larva does most of the damage. Caterpillars can strip a field in days.

Incomplete change (three stages)

Egg, nymph, adult. The nymph looks like a small adult without full wings.

  • Grasshoppers and locusts, aphids, stink bugs, whitefly, thrips.
  • Both nymphs and adults cause damage.

Damage you can see

DamagePossible pest
Holes in leaves, eaten edgesCaterpillars, beetles, grasshoppers, snails
Ragged leaves and sawdust-like droppings in maize whorlsFall armyworm, stalk borer
Curled, yellow leaves, sticky honeydew, black sooty mouldAphids, whitefly, mealybug, scale
Silver streaks or scarred fruitThrips
Holes in fruit, soft rotten patches with maggotsFruit fly, codling moth
Plants wilting, roots eaten or knottedCutworms, white grubs, nematodes
Speckled pale leaves with fine websRed spider mite

When you find damage, look for the pest itself nearby: under leaves, inside the maize whorl, in the soil at the base of wilting plants, or inside the fruit. Old damage with no pests may already be over; fresh damage with living pests needs quick action.

Damage from sucking insects can also spread virus diseases from plant to plant.

lessons.title: Diseases, weeds and scouting
lessons.html:
What causes plant diseases?

  • Fungi: the most common. Signs are spots, powdery or fluffy mould, rust-coloured pustules, rot. Examples: rust on wheat, early blight on tomatoes and potatoes, powdery mildew.
  • Bacteria: wet, slimy or smelly rots, wilting, leaf spots with yellow edges.
  • Viruses: mottled yellow-green leaves, curling, stunted plants. Often spread by aphids or whitefly.

Basic life cycle of a fungal disease

  1. Spores land on the plant (blown by wind, splashed by rain, carried on tools or people).
  2. With moisture and the right temperature, spores grow into the plant.
  3. The fungus spreads inside and causes symptoms.
  4. It makes new spores that spread to other plants.

This is why many diseases spread fast in warm, wet weather.

Weeds

A weed is a plant growing where it is not wanted. Weeds take water, light and nutrients from crops, and can host pests and diseases. Common weeds include nutgrass, blackjacks, khakibos and pigweed. Some are declared invaders that must be controlled by law under the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983.

How pests, diseases and weeds spread

  • Wind, rain splash and irrigation water.
  • Insects carrying viruses.
  • People, tools, tractors and implements carrying soil, seeds and spores between lands.
  • Infected seed and seedlings.
  • Animals and birds carrying weed seeds.

Scouting

  1. Walk the land in a set pattern (for example a W or zigzag), as your supervisor shows.
  2. Stop at set points and check a number of plants: top and underside of leaves, stems, flowers, fruit, roots.
  3. Check traps (for example fruit fly or moth traps) and count the catch.
  4. Write down: land, date, plant checked, what you found, how many, and beneficial insects seen.
  5. Report to your supervisor the same day.

Key points

  • Insects have three body parts, six legs and two antennae.
  • Not all insects are pests; protect beneficial insects.
  • Insects grow by complete (four-stage) or incomplete (three-stage) change.
  • Fungi, bacteria and viruses cause plant diseases.
  • Scout in a pattern, record carefully and report the same day.
